items.title: Cromwell did not set out to be a republican
items.claim: What were Oliver Cromwell's politics in 1642?

options.text: He had been a republican agitator since the 1620s
He was a Huntingdonshire MP and country gentleman who fought for Parliament against the king's policies but moved towards regicide only by late 1648
He was a paid Dutch agent from the start
He was a Leveller from the outset

items.reveal:
Cromwell entered the 1640 Long Parliament as MP for Cambridge. As late as 1647 he was negotiating with Charles I (the Heads of the Proposals). The king's plotting with the Scots — the Second Civil War of 1648 — convinced Cromwell that Charles could not be trusted.

Pride's Purge (December 1648) removed MPs likely to negotiate. The Rump Parliament tried and executed the king on 30 January 1649. Cromwell signed the death warrant but had not been pushing for it years earlier.

He later dissolved the Rump (1653) and accepted the title Lord Protector, refusing the crown in 1657.
items.why: The 'inevitable republican' Cromwell of memory is partly constructed by 19th-century liberals (Macaulay, Carlyle). The actual man's politics shifted under pressure of events.

items.title: Clause 39 of Magna Carta is the ancestor of due process
items.claim: What does Clause 39 of Magna Carta (1215) say?

options.text: 'No free man shall be seized or imprisoned, or stripped of his rights or possessions... except by the lawful judgment of his equals or by the law of the land' — the basis of habeas corpus and due process traditions

items.reveal:
The 1215 charter had 63 clauses, mostly about specific feudal grievances. Clause 39 (combined with clause 40 — 'to no one will we sell, to no one deny or delay right or justice') is the source of the due process tradition.

'Free man' (liber homo) in 1215 was a small minority — perhaps a tenth of the population. The protection was extended over centuries by reissue, interpretation and common-law development.

The US Fifth Amendment (1791) — 'nor be deprived of life, liberty, or property, without due process of law' — directly echoes Magna Carta. The phrase 'due process of law' was first used in a 1354 reissue of the charter under Edward III.
items.why: Founding documents have specific clauses that travel further than others. Clause 39 of Magna Carta is the single most influential sentence in English-language constitutional law — its 21st-century echoes are direct.

items.title: The Korean War never formally ended
items.claim: How did the Korean War conclude?

options.text: An armistice signed at Panmunjom on 27 July 1953 by representatives of the UN Command, North Korea and China — but no peace treaty; the Koreas remain technically at war and the DMZ at the 38th parallel divides them

items.reveal:
Armistice negotiations began in July 1951 and lasted two years, largely over the issue of prisoner repatriation. South Korean President Syngman Rhee refused to sign and unilaterally released 27,000 North Korean POWs in June 1953.

The Korean Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) is 4 km wide and around 250 km long — one of the most heavily militarised borders in the world. Periodic incidents (the 1968 capture of USS Pueblo, the 2010 Yeonpyeong shelling) keep the conflict warm.

Moves toward a formal peace declaration have repeatedly stalled. The Korean War cost around 3 million lives — Korean civilians the majority — and shaped East Asian security for over 70 years.
items.why: Unresolved conflicts shape decades. The absence of a Korean peace treaty in 1953 is the structural foundation of every subsequent crisis on the peninsula.
